description_ru: Антиквар и покупательница торгуются за «подлинные» напольные часы. Каждый играет роль, но настоящий вопрос в том, кто кого обманывает. Лукавый диалог с ироничной развязкой.
text:
Pettifer: Ah, madam, I see you have found the Lancashire. A rare moment in any dealer's life: the instant when a customer's eye meets an object across a crowded shop and something passes between them. I will not insult it by speaking. I shall simply stand over here and be moved.
Calloway: You may stand wherever you like, Mr. Pettifer, but you will have to be moved at a lower volume. I am interested in the grandfather clock, and I should like to know why the label says "circa 1740" in handwriting that looks suspiciously like it was done last Thursday.

Pettifer: Circa, madam, is a word of enormous elasticity. In the antiques trade it can mean anything from a century to a decade, depending on the mood of the buyer and the humidity. But I assure you, this is a genuine article. The case is oak, the dial is brass, and the movement bears the name of a maker in Wigan whose descendants, I believe, still sell clocks, though not of this quality.
Calloway: Genuine. Let us explore that word. I notice the screws that hold the hood in place are slotted, evenly cut, with perfectly uniform threads. In 1740, I understand, screws were filed by hand and each one looked like a small, tragic accident.

Pettifer: Ah. A woman of observation. Those, madam, are replacements, installed by a conscientious restorer who feared for the structural integrity of the case. One must distinguish, in this trade, between authenticity and mere corrosion. A genuine antique is one that has been loved, and therefore occasionally repaired.
Calloway: I see. And the key to the case door, which has the unmistakable sheen of something that came out of a hardware shop in Stockport last week?

Pettifer: A key is a key, madam. It opens a door. It does not bear witness to the century. If I were to be so rash as to produce a key from 1740, it would be corroded, and it would not open anything at all, and you would be justifiably annoyed.
Calloway: Mr. Pettifer, you are a man of formidable resourcefulness. Let me tell you why I ask these questions. My late husband owned a clock very like this one. He told me, on his deathbed, with the grave expression of a man confessing to a crime, that he had bought it from a Mr. Pettifer in the autumn of 1998 for four thousand pounds, and that it had stopped working the following Tuesday.

Pettifer: Ah. Hm. That would have been my father, madam. A different Pettifer entirely. A man of impulsive character and weak ethics. I have spent a good deal of my life atoning for him.
Calloway: Your father was, I believe, also named Reginald, and also wore a green waistcoat with a small tear under the left pocket.

Pettifer: Family resemblance is a powerful thing, madam. It is the reason so many of us have the same nose.
Calloway: It is also, I observe, the reason so many of us have the same habit of lying with a perfectly straight face. My husband had it too. He told me, for thirty years, that he was a collector of fine clocks, when in truth he collected only the excuses for buying them. The shed at the bottom of our garden contains eleven, each of them wrong by a different amount, like a congregation of very old and very stubborn relatives.

Pettifer: Then I salute his memory, madam. He had the true collector's temperament, which is to say, an incurable optimism about the future value of things that stopped working in the past. A man like that is the backbone of my business. I should like to have known him better, and I regret that my father knew him slightly too well. Still, madam, you wound me, and with a skill I can only admire. Let me be frank, for once, as a gesture of professional goodwill. Half of what I sell is not the object at all. It is the story that comes with it. A customer who buys a clock believes he is acquiring a past, a small private heirloom with a lineage, and I merely supply the lineage. It is a kind of poetry, and you may call it fraud only if you are willing to call every novelist a liar.
Calloway: I am willing to call every novelist a liar, Mr. Pettifer, and I shall continue to read them with enormous pleasure. But novelists, I notice, put the word "fiction" on the cover. Which brings me back to the label.

Pettifer: Madam, I have a new label coming from the printer next week, and it reads, in a tasteful italic, "A faithful reproduction, in the manner of 1740". I had it made after your husband's visit, in a fit of remorse. I merely have not had the courage to put it out.
Calloway: Then you are a better man than your father, and an inferior forger. But I have no wish to embarrass you, Mr. Pettifer. I came here not for a refund, but for an offer. That clock, the one that stopped in 1998, was, as I discovered, a very fine reproduction made in a factory in Birmingham in 1962. And I have spent a year learning the difference between a copy and an original, because I enjoy it. I have been to auctions, spoken to restorers, and read three books, one of them in German. I know precisely what I am looking at.

Pettifer: Then, madam, you will have recognised that the piece before you is, in fact, an honest reproduction, made in Birmingham in the nineteen-sixties, which I have been offering at a perfectly fair price for a perfectly decorative object.
Calloway: Honest. How refreshing. I wonder, then, whether we might discuss a price that reflects the honesty. Say, three hundred pounds? And a small discount, since the label was misleading, in the interest of mutual transparency.

Pettifer: Three hundred? Madam, it is a clock! It has a case, a face, and a pendulum! I paid two hundred and fifty for it myself, in a sale of the estate of a person of enormous wealth and indifferent taste.
Calloway: Then three hundred leaves you a profit, and a clear conscience, which you will admit is more than my husband received. And I shall pay in cash, so that nobody need write anything down. I understand that is your preferred method of settling disputes.

Pettifer: Madam, I believe we have discovered, at last, the beginning of a beautiful friendship. Allow me to wrap it. And if I may be so bold, should you ever find yourself in the market for a genuine Georgian sideboard, I happen to know a man.

questions.question: What is the clock labelled as?
What does Mrs. Calloway say about her late husband?
questions.answer: He bought a clock from Pettifer's father that stopped working a week later.

questions.question: What is the truth about the clock?
questions.answer: It is a reproduction made in Birmingham in the 1960s.
